item.title: How to stay consistent with calorie tracking: 6 rules
item.description: Six rules from habit research, with sample sizes. Health habits took a median of 59 to 66 days to feel automatic, and 4 to 335 days across people.
item.content:encoded:
Two things in the research move food logging from a chore into something you just do: a fixed event to hang it on, and a low bar for what counts as a day logged. In the one review that pooled the question, health habits took a median of 59 to 66 days to feel automatic, with individual times from 4 to 335 days (Singh et al., Healthcare 2024, 20 studies, 2,601 participants).

The low bar matters more than it sounds. In an 8 week study of 90 adults using a food app, every week with three or more days logged was worth 0.23% of body weight, while recording at least half of your calorie goal predicted nothing at all (Payne et al., 2022).

I read six papers for this on 27 October 2026 and pulled six rules out of them. Where a number comes from a review rather than the original paper, I say so.

What are the six rules?

Hang the log on something you already do early in the day, and keep the bar at three days a week. Each rule below comes from one study, with its sample size.

Rule Study and sample What it measured What it found
Plan for two months, not three weeks Singh 2024, review of 20 studies, 2,601 people Days to reach automaticity Medians of 59 and 66 days, individuals 4 to 335
Put it in the morning Fournier 2017, via Singh 2024 Daily stretching, morning vs evening Mean 106 days morning, 154 days evening
Hang it on the end of a routine you already have Judah 2013, N = 50 Flossing before vs after brushing Flossing after brushing gave stronger habits at 8 months
Use the event, not the clock Stawarz 2015, 4 week study plus 115 apps Reminders vs event based cues Reminders gave repetition, event cues gave automaticity
Clear three days a week before chasing accuracy Payne 2022, n = 90, 8 weeks Consistency vs completeness 0.23% of weight per consistent week, completeness p = 0.062
Spread it over two or three visits a day Harvey 2019, n = 142, 24 weeks Journal visits a day at month six 2.7 a day for the biggest losers, 1.7 for the rest

How long before logging feels automatic?

About two months for a typical person, and anywhere from a few days to most of a year for a real one. Most of the useful information is in that spread.

Singh and colleagues searched six databases and found 20 experimental studies covering 2,601 people (Healthcare 2024). Only four of those reported how long a habit took to form.

Keller 2021 put healthy eating habits at a median of 59 days with a range of 4 to 335, and only 23% of participants got there at all. Lally 2010 reported a median of 66 days, Lally 2008 a mean of 91 days, and Fournier 2017 a mean of 106 days for morning stretching against 154 for evening. All four figures come from the 2024 review, which I read in full; I could not open the Lally papers themselves.

The 21 day figure that every habit article repeats is in none of them.

Does it matter when in the day I log?

Earlier is better, and immediately after something you already do is better still. Two studies point the same way from different behaviours.

Fournier's stretchers took 48 days longer to reach automaticity in the evening than in the morning, as reported in Singh's review. Mornings have fewer competing events, so the cue fires before the day can bury it.

Judah and colleagues gave all 50 participants the same motivational session, then told half to floss before brushing and half after. Those who flossed after brushing had stronger habits and flossed more often at the 8 month follow up (Judah et al., 2013).

So pick the end of an existing routine rather than a time. "After I pour the first coffee" beats "in the morning".

Why do reminders stop working?

Because an alarm trains you to answer the alarm, not to notice the meal. That is the uncomfortable result in the one study that compared the two directly.

Stawarz, Cox and Blandford ran a 4 week cue study and reviewed 115 habit apps for CHI 2015. Reminders supported repetition but "hindered habit development", while "event-based cues led to increased automaticity", and positive reinforcement did nothing (Bristol repository record).

One 4 week study is not a law, and a reminder you act on beats a habit you never form. Our reminder comparison found that at best 19.05% of logging reminders were tapped, which is about what you would expect from a cue with no event attached.

The practical version of an event cue is an if then sentence written in advance. Across 23 eating studies, those plans had a Cohen's d of 0.51 for adding healthy foods and 0.29 for cutting unhealthy ones (Adriaanse et al., Appetite 2011).

Is it better to log everything, or to log something every day?

Something, every few days. Logging roughly on three days a week predicted weight loss; logging your full calorie goal did not.

Payne and colleagues followed 90 employees with overweight or obesity for 8 weeks on Calorie Counter by FatSecret (Obes Sci Pract 2022). They scored three kinds of adherence: frequency, consistency (weeks with three or more days logged) and completeness (weeks recording at least half the calorie goal).

Consistency and frequency both predicted weight change, at 0.23% of body weight per consistent week and 0.02% per extra 1% of days. Completeness missed significance at p = 0.062 (regression results).

Participants averaged 4.4 consistent weeks out of 8 (Payne 2022). Running their slope out, the gap between 2 consistent weeks and all 8 is 1.38% of body weight, about 1.3 kg at this group's mean weight of 94.9 kg.

Two honest caveats, both from the same paper. Among the 50 people who finished the full 8 weeks, none of the three measures reached significance, and 89% of the sample backlogged at least one day rather than logging it live (results section).

How many times a day should I log?

Two or three, in small visits. Minutes spent did not separate the people who lost weight; the number of separate visits did.

Harvey and colleagues tracked 142 people through a 24 week online weight programme. Time spent self monitoring fell from 23.2 minutes a day in month 1 to 18.1 in month 3 and 14.6 in month 6, and 65.5% were still recording anything by then (Obesity 2019).

At month six, those who had lost 5% or more of their weight opened the journal 2.4 times a day against 1.6 for the rest, and the 10% group 2.7 against 1.7, both at p below 0.001 (Harvey et al., Obesity 2019). The authors' own reading is that successful participants logged "at least two to three times a day".

Average those three figures and you get 18.6 minutes a day, which over 24 weeks is about 52 hours of typing. That is the real price of the method, and it is why the effort side matters as much as the cue side.

52 hoursof logging over six months, at the minutes a day this trial measuredHarvey et al., 2019

Where does MealSaid fit, and where does it fail this test?

It cuts the cost of one entry; it does not give you a proper event cue. I built it, so take the second half seriously.

MealSaid calls your phone at times you choose and asks what you ate. That is a clock cue, the exact kind Stawarz found builds repetition rather than automaticity, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

What it does help with is the three days a week bar. You say the meal in one sentence and it lands in Apple Health, or you say it to Siri with the app closed, which is how you attach a log to a real event like putting the plate in the sink. There is more on the mechanics in how MealSaid works.

It has no barcode scanner, no photo logging, no food database search and no way to import food other apps wrote to Apple Health. It is iPhone only and needs iOS 26. It understands English only. If you want a database you can audit, Cronometer is the better tool and this is not a close call.

For why the quitting happens in the first place, I went through seven dropout studies in why people quit calorie tracking.

How I checked this

Checked 27 October 2026. I read the Singh 2024 review, the Payne 2022 paper and the Harvey 2019 paper in full on PubMed Central, the Judah 2013 abstract on the authors' own repository at LSHTM, the Stawarz 2015 abstract on the University of Bristol research record, and the Adriaanse 2011 abstract through its publisher page.

Four numbers are second hand and labelled as such: the Keller 2021, Lally 2010, Lally 2008 and Fournier 2017 formation times, all taken from Singh's review because the original papers sit behind publisher walls that refuse automated access. The 52 hour figure and the 1.38% gap are my own arithmetic on the published means and regression slopes, not findings from the papers.

Nothing here is from MealSaid's own data. I have not published an adherence study of my own yet. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Can I log food by talking to an app? I checked 22
item.description: Eleven of 21 iPhone food trackers document saying what you ate, checked 27 October 2026. Three take the meal through Siri with the app still shut.
item.content:encoded:
Yes, on 11 of the 21 iPhone food trackers I checked, plus my own. Eight of those eleven describe taking a whole spoken meal rather than one food at a time, and three apps take the meal through Siri while the app stays shut.

I read every one of those App Store listings and help pages on 27 October 2026. The listings came from Apple's own lookup service, which also gives the date each one was last changed, and that date turned out to matter.

One app contradicts itself. Lose It's listing was updated on 26 October 2026, the day before I read it, to claim whole meal voice logging, while its own help article from August still describes voice as a way to search for one food.

Which iPhone apps can you actually talk to?

Eleven of 21, and MealSaid makes twelve. Nine of those twelve, mine included, say the app takes a whole spoken meal; ten apps say nothing about voice at all.

App What you can say Where it is documented Date on that page
MyFitnessPal A whole meal, Premium only Help article 21 Sep 2026
Lose It! Listing says a whole meal, help page says a food search Listing, help 26 Oct and 25 Aug 2026
Cronometer A whole meal on Gold, and a Siri phrase Help article 26 Oct 2026
MyNetDiary A whole meal on Premium Plus, plain voice free Listing 26 Oct 2026
MacroFactor A whole meal, typed or spoken, inside Describe Help article No date shown
Lifesum A whole meal on Premium Listing 23 Oct 2026
MacrosFirst A whole meal, and a Siri phrase on Premium Help article No date shown
Foodvisor A whole meal, spoken to the app Listing 22 Oct 2026
SnapCalorie A dictated voice note Listing 8 Oct 2026
BiteSnap Voice, with no detail given Listing 10 Oct 2025
Carb Manager Voice logging, called Say, on Premium, no detail Help article 10 Jul 2026
MealSaid A whole meal, free, and a Siri phrase How it works 27 Oct 2026

Prices are in our voice input comparison rather than repeated here, because they move faster than the features do.

What happens after you stop talking?

Two things, depending on the app: a list of matched foods you approve, or a search result you still pick from. Nothing in this field saves your words without showing you a guess first.

MyFitnessPal is the plainest about it. Its help article says "Voice Logging lets you say what you ate and get it into your diary", then walks you through tapping each food to fix the serving before tapping Log (MyFitnessPal, 21 September 2026).

Cronometer describes the same shape, as a feature that lets you "dictate or type out a description of the food you are eating" and returns matched foods to review (Cronometer, 26 October 2026).

Two apps claim voice and leave it there. Carb Manager's Premium page lists "Say (voice logging)" with no explanation, and BiteSnap's listing calls itself a voice enabled food tracker and stops.

MacroFactor is honest that the microphone is incidental. "Just type (or speak) a description of your food or meal", says its logging guide, which is the keyboard doing the speaking and the search doing the work (MacroFactor).

Which apps take the meal without opening the app?

Cronometer on Gold, MacrosFirst on Premium, and MealSaid. All three go through a Siri phrase, so the screen never has to come up.

Cronometer's Siri article, updated 24 October 2026, walks you through turning on its shortcut and then saying "Log food in Cronometer", after which Siri asks what you ate (Cronometer).

MacrosFirst does the same for Premium users, "all through Siri without ever opening the app", and handles serving size inside the Siri conversation (MacrosFirst).

Everyone else puts the microphone behind a screen. I counted the actual touches for each route in the hands free post.

Why do two of Lose It's own pages disagree?

Because the App Store listing was rewritten on 26 October 2026 and the help article has not caught up since 25 August. That is 62 days between two pages from the same company saying different things.

The listing now puts "Say 'I had 2 eggs, toast with butter and jam' to log your meal" under Premium plan features (Lose It, US App Store).

The help article still tells you to "use Say It to search for a food by voice", then pick the food, the serving unit and the quantity (Lose It help, 25 August 2026).

I am taking the listing as the newer fact and the help article as the one to watch. If you are paying for Lose It Premium to say whole meals, try it before the renewal lands.

Apple's lookup service returns the listing text and a last updated date for any App Store id, which is how the dates above were read without a browser. It is the same data Apple shows on the product page.

Which apps do not let you talk at all?

Cal AI, Yazio, Noom, FatSecret, Nutritionix Track, Simple, Fastic, Zero, AteMate and MyPlate. None of them mentions voice or Siri on any page I could open.

Cal AI is the notable one, because it sells itself on effortless logging. Its listing of 20 October 2026 offers a photo of your meal and a typed description, and never a spoken one (Cal AI, US App Store).

FatSecret belongs in this column with an asterisk. Its listing of 6 October 2026 says nothing about voice, and its help centre returns 403 to every automated fetch I tried, so I am not going to describe a page I could not read.

BiteSnap sits at the other edge. Its listing calls it a "voice-enabled food tracker" and stops there, and that listing has not changed since 10 October 2025 (BiteSnap, US App Store).

Which one should I talk to?

If you already pay for a tracker, use the voice feature you bought; if you are starting fresh, decide first whether you want Siri or an in app microphone. That single choice removes most of the list.

For Siri with the app shut, the paid answer is Cronometer Gold, and it has the deepest nutrient data of anything here. Cronometer is the better tool if you want numbers you can audit, and I say that as a competitor.

MealSaid is my free answer to the same question. You say what you ate, it estimates calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber and writes them to Apple Health, and a Siri phrase does it with the app closed.

It has no barcode scanner, no photo logging, no food database to browse and no restaurant menus. It is iPhone only and needs iOS 26, and it understands English only. Wrong app for a household that logs packaged food by barcode.

How I checked this

Checked 27 October 2026. I built the list by running US App Store searches for the names people use for calorie apps, keeping every general food or calorie tracker that came back, then reading each listing through Apple's lookup service and each company's own help centre.

Help centre dates come from the Zendesk timestamps on the MyFitnessPal, Lose It and Cronometer articles, read through those help centres' own article endpoints because the web pages return 403 to scripts, and from the published date on the Carb Manager page. MacroFactor and MacrosFirst show no date on their help pages, so those two rows say so rather than guessing.

Two gaps. FatSecret's help pages refused every request, so FatSecret sits in the no voice column rather than being described from a page I could not open. I did not install these apps or time them, so every row here is documentation reading, not a hands on test, and my own app is the only one I can speak about from use.

Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Hands-free calorie tracking while cooking or driving
item.description: Three iPhone apps log a meal with zero touches. MyFitnessPal needs five and Lose It needs eight, counted from their own steps on 26 October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Three iPhone calorie apps log a meal without you touching the phone at all: Cronometer on Gold, MacrosFirst on Premium, and MealSaid, which I built and which is free. All three work through a Siri phrase, so the app never opens. Every other voice feature I checked makes you tap at least twice after you stop talking.

I counted the touches in each app's own step list on 26 October 2026. MyFitnessPal's Voice Log takes five touches from a locked phone to a saved entry, Cronometer's in-app voice logging takes five, and Lose It's Say It takes eight.

None of them work through the car screen, mine included. Apple's CarPlay category list has no slot for food logging.

What counts as hands-free?

Two moments decide it: whether you can start without touching the phone, and whether you can finish without touching it. Most voice features only solve the middle.

Turning speech into text is the easy part. Every app below does that well enough once you are already on its logging screen.

The cost sits at the two ends. You tap your way in, then you tap to confirm the match, and both taps want a dry finger and a look at the screen.

Which apps log a meal with zero touches?

Three, and all three use a Siri phrase instead of a button inside the app.

App Start without touching the phone Finish without touching the phone Documented to work when locked What it costs
MealSaid Yes, "log in MealSaid" plus the meal Yes, Siri shows a card Yes, in my step by step post Free
Cronometer Yes, "Log food in Cronometer" Yes, Siri asks which foods, a banner confirms Not stated Gold
MacrosFirst Yes, "Log food in MacrosFirst" Yes, serving and meal handled in Siri Not stated Premium
MyFitnessPal No, three touches before you speak No, the arrow and then Log No Premium
Lose It! No, four touches before you speak No, four touches after No Not stated in the article
MacroFactor No, Describe lives inside the app No, you confirm the plate No Paid app

Cronometer is the one to look at if you want this on a mature tracker. Its article says Gold iOS users can log "without having to open the app", and that a banner confirms the item (Cronometer support, updated 24 October 2026).

MacrosFirst does the same for Premium users and handles serving size and meal in the Siri conversation, "all through Siri without ever opening the app" (MacrosFirst help). Its Log Food shortcut rides on AI Search, which its page calls a Premium feature.

Whether a phrase survives a locked phone is a choice the developer makes, not luck. Apple's App Intents framework has an authentication policy per action, and the alwaysAllowed case lets an action "run at any time, including when the device is locked" (Apple developer documentation).

Why does the tap after you speak matter?

Because that is the tap you cannot make with oil on your fingers. It is also the one that pulls your eyes back to the screen.

MyFitnessPal's iOS steps are open the app, tap the plus, tap Voice Log, speak, tap the blue arrow, tap Log. Voice Log is Premium, English only, and needs app version 24.35.0 or higher (MyFitnessPal help, updated 21 September 2026).

Cronometer's in-app route is shorter at five: the plus menu, Voice-Logging, speak, Match Foods, Add To Diary (Cronometer support, updated 24 October 2026).

Lose It is the longest of the group. Its article runs Log, Add Food, Say It, pick the food, pick a serving unit and quantity, Add or Save, then Done, and notes that Say It is English only (Lose It help, updated 25 August 2026).

MacroFactor's Describe accepts speech, in one parenthesis: "Just type (or speak) a description of your food or meal" (MacroFactor help). I found no Siri phrase for it in their help centre.

I searched the Lose It and MyFitnessPal help centres for "Siri" on 26 October 2026 and both returned zero articles. For a route comparison that includes widgets and the Lock Screen, see the post on logging without opening an app.

Can I log calories while driving?

Not through the car screen. Apple's CarPlay page names eleven kinds of app, and food logging is not one of them.

Apple's wording is about tasks you do on the way somewhere: EV charging, fueling, parking, public safety and quick food ordering "can help people accomplish important tasks without taking out their phone" (Apple CarPlay for developers). Ordering a burrito is a category. Recording that you ate one is not.

That leaves Siri on the phone, and it is worth being honest about what that costs. AAA had 120 drivers use the built-in systems of 30 model year 2017 cars, and rated 23 of the 30 at high or very high demand (AAA Foundation, 2017).

23 of 30cars whose built-in systems rated high or very high demand with 120 driversAAA Foundation 2017

The useful detail for us is the direction. Voice lowered visual demand against the other modes, but the interactions ran longer, and the longer time cancelled the gain. A one-sentence log is near the short end of that range; anything that makes you read a list of matches is not, and should wait until you park.

What works when my hands are covered in oil?

A spoken Siri phrase, and after that the accessibility settings. Cooking is the easier case because you can look at the screen, you just cannot touch it.

Four things to set up once, in this order:

  1. Settings, then Apple Intelligence & Siri, then Talk to Siri, so the phrase works without the side button. Cronometer's article walks through the same screens.
  2. Settings, Accessibility, Siri. Cronometer's page points here for pause time and for the Always Listen option, which it says lets Siri listen while the phone is locked.
  3. AirPods, if the phone is across the kitchen. The phrase is the same and the microphone is nearer your mouth.
  4. For an app with no Siri phrase at all, Voice Control. Apple's page describes speaking commands "just like you would perform an action by touch", and the Show names command puts labels on everything tappable (Apple Support).

Voice Control is the slow option because you say the name of every button, and it is the only one that works on apps that shipped no voice support. It was built for people who cannot use a touchscreen, which is also the situation you are in with flour on both hands.

Where MealSaid is the wrong answer

It is a talking app with nothing behind it to browse. My own gaps, in the same spirit as the table.

  • No CarPlay app, for the reason above, and no Android.
  • No barcode scanner, no photo logging, no food database to search and no restaurant menus.
  • iOS 26 and English only, and the phrase needs a connection, because the understanding happens on our server rather than on the phone.

Cronometer is the better choice if you want a verified database and a confirmation step before anything lands in your diary. Its own note recommends reviewing Siri-logged foods the next time you open the app, which is a fair warning that every app in this category should print.

How I checked this

Checked 26 October 2026. I read each company's own help article and counted the touches in its numbered steps, treating "open the app" as one touch and ignoring permission prompts and anything a saved meal would let you skip. The Cronometer, MyFitnessPal and Lose It articles are dated inside their help centres and I have quoted those dates above. The MacrosFirst and MacroFactor pages carry no visible date.

Two things I could not verify. Lose It's App Store description no longer mentions Say It at all, so I am not repeating the Premium label I used for it in an earlier post, and its logging article does not say which tier Say It belongs to. Neither Cronometer nor MacrosFirst states whether its Siri action runs on a locked phone, so those cells say "not stated" rather than "no".

I did not install the competitors for this post, and I did not time anything on a real phone; these are document counts. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Calorie tracker for ADHD, counted by decisions per meal
item.description: No app treats ADHD. Logging one food takes 6 choices in Lose It, 5 in MyFitnessPal, 4 in Cronometer and 1 if you say the meal out loud.
item.content:encoded:
There is no calorie tracker built for ADHD, and no app is a treatment for it. What an app can change is the number of decisions one entry costs, and that varies more than the marketing does: logging a single food takes six choices in Lose It, five in MyFitnessPal, four in Cronometer, and one if you say the whole meal out loud.

I counted those from each company's own help page on 26 October 2026. Then I read the research on why decisions, rather than taps, are the part that breaks.

One thing up front. The research below is about populations, not about you, and none of it shows that ADHD causes anything about weight.

Is there a calorie tracker made for ADHD?

No, and I would be wary of one that said it was. None of the apps I checked claims a clinical result, and none has been tested in an ADHD population.

What you can compare is friction, and four things carry most of it.

  1. How many separate choices one entry costs.
  2. Whether anything reaches you before the meal is forgotten.
  3. Whether a missed day or a bad number punishes you when you open the app.
  4. Whether you can log at 11pm for a lunch that happened at 1pm.

The numbers below cover the first two, which are the ones I could count from documents.

What does the research show about ADHD and eating?

A steady association with weight, a stronger one with eating disorders, and no evidence of cause in either direction.

The obesity figure comes from Cortese and colleagues, who pooled 42 studies covering 728,136 people. For adults the odds ratio was 1.55 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.81), and pooled obesity prevalence was 28.2% in adults with ADHD against 16.4% in those without (Am J Psychiatry 2016).

28.2% vs 16.4%pooled obesity prevalence in adults with and without ADHD, 42 studiesCortese et al., 2016

The same review reports that "individuals medicated for ADHD were not at higher risk of obesity", which is a useful brake on any story that treats this as a willpower gap (Am J Psychiatry 2016).

The eating disorder numbers are larger and matter more for how you use a tracker. Nazar and colleagues pooled 12 studies (4,013 people with ADHD against 29,404 controls) and found odds of 3.82 for any eating disorder, 4.13 for binge eating disorder, and 2.57 the other way round in 5 studies of eating disorder cohorts (Int J Eat Disord 2016).

That is my reason for saying something uncomfortable about my own category. If counting makes you restrict, a calorie app is the wrong tool, and the odds above say that applies to more people here than average. For scale, the CDC estimated 15.5 million US adults (6.0%) had a current ADHD diagnosis in 2023, from 7,046 interviews (MMWR, 10 October 2024).

How many decisions does one food entry take?

Six in Lose It, five in MyFitnessPal, four in Cronometer, one if you say the meal.

I counted a decision as any point where the app's own instructions ask you to pick between alternatives for this one food. Tapping a fixed button is not a decision. Picking which search result is your yoghurt is.

Lose It's article runs meal, tab (Search, My Foods, Meals or Recipes), search words, food, serving unit, quantity (Lose It help, updated 25 August 2026).

MyFitnessPal's runs meal, search words, result, serving size, number of servings (MyFitnessPal help, updated 23 October 2026).

Cronometer is the lightest of the three at four, because meal and quantity live on one screen: search words, food, serving size, diary group (Cronometer support, updated 25 October 2026). Cronometer does this better than the two bigger apps, and it is free for that route.

This is a different count from the one in my post on Cronometer's step list, which counted steps. Steps include the taps you do on autopilot. Decisions are the ones that need your attention back on the meal.

Why do decisions matter more than taps?

Because every decision asks you to hold the meal in mind while you answer something else. Lose the thread between "chicken burrito" and "which of these burritos", and the entry does not happen.

Cordeiro and colleagues surveyed 141 food journalers (47 active, 94 lapsed) alongside 5,526 forum posts. Their line on missed entries is blunt: "Simply forgetting to journal is a major barrier", and it was the most cited reason respondents had missed at least one. Asked what made journaling hard, 31 called it too much effort, 27 called it time consuming and 16 called it tedious (CHI 2015).

The same paper describes the other failure: people who had a bad day stopped opening the app, because red numbers read like a verdict. No app I checked lets you turn that off.

Study Who What it found Link
Cordeiro et al., 2015 141 journalers, 47 active and 94 lapsed, plus 5,526 forum posts Forgetting was the most cited reason for a missed entry; 31 respondents called journaling too much effort CHI 2015 PDF
Patel et al., 2022 38 adults randomized, 18 detailed and 20 simplified, 3 month program Simplified logging got 97% of days against 49%, with the same weight loss (3.3 kg vs 3.4 kg) JMIR Form Res
Chen et al., 2024 30 people, 4 weeks, each person tried both prompt types, Android Context triggered prompts: 21.77% logged within an hour against 17.32% for fixed-time prompts CHI 2024 PDF
Cavero-Redondo et al., 2020 Meta-analysis of 20 studies Phone based self-monitoring held adherence better than paper at six and twelve months Nutrients

Patel's trial is the one that moves me most. Eighteen people logged every food in the Fitbit app and twenty ticked a daily checklist of high calorie foods; median days logged were 49% against 97%, and weight change was the same, 3.4 kg against 3.3 kg (JMIR Form Res 2022). Thirty-eight people is a pilot, not a verdict.

Do reminders fix the forgetting?

Partly, and less than you would hope. Chen and colleagues gave 30 people four weeks of both prompt types, and context triggered prompts were followed by a log within the hour 21.77% of the time against 17.32% for fixed-time ones (CHI 2024).

Read that as the ceiling for a banner. Four in five prompts went unanswered in the better condition, because a notification still asks you to go and do the six decisions. That study ran on Android phones, so treat the size of the gap as a direction rather than a number for iPhones.

MealSaid's answer is to make the interruption harder to dismiss: at times you pick, your phone rings like a normal call and a voice asks what you ate. Whether that beats a banner over a month is exactly the test I have not published yet, and I am not going to claim it until I have. The longer version of the dropout research is in why most people quit calorie tracking.

Where MealSaid is not the answer

It is one sentence per meal and nothing else, which is a feature until it is not.

  • No barcode scanner and no database you can browse, so a packaged food you cannot name is a guess.
  • iOS 26 and English only, and the phrase needs a connection because the understanding happens on our server.
  • It estimates from your sentence. If you want gram-level control and a full micronutrient profile, Cronometer is the better app and I would say so to anyone.

And the thing that no app covers: if logging tips into counting that feels compulsive, stop and talk to a clinician rather than switching apps. The Nazar numbers above are the reason that sentence is in this post.

How I checked this

Checked 26 October 2026. The decision counts come from each company's current help article, read on that date, counting only the choices the instructions name for a single food, and ignoring the shortcuts (saved meals, favourites, recents) that cut every count. The research numbers come from the PubMed abstracts and open PDFs linked above, read the same day, and each one carries its sample size in the table or the sentence.

What I could not do. There is no study of calorie tracking apps in an ADHD population that I could find, so the friction argument here is an inference from general logging research, not a tested claim about ADHD. I also have no adherence data of my own yet; the 30 day comparison of reminders against a scheduled call is running on one person, which is me, and that is a weak design I will label as such when it goes up.

Corrections and better papers to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: A simpler Cronometer alternative: I counted the steps
item.description: Cronometer's own help page lists 4 steps to log a food, Lose It lists 9. Five simpler alternatives with prices and step counts, checked 25 Oct 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Cronometer's own instructions for logging one food are four steps long, shorter than MyFitnessPal's six and Lose It's nine. The simpler swap most people are looking for is MyNetDiary, whose core version is "free and ad-free", tracks 108 nutrients and takes a spoken sentence in five published steps.

The weight in Cronometer sits inside those four steps: seven category tabs, a Sort By menu, a database filter and a Better Alternative swap, all described on the same help page.

Cronometer has its own fast route, a spoken sentence, and it costs $59.99 a year.

I read five help centres and four App Store listings on 25 October 2026 and counted the steps each company publishes. I build a calorie tracker, so treat the second to last section as the biased one.

How many steps does Cronometer take to log one food?

Four, by its own count: tap the plus icon, tap Add Food, type the name, tap the food to open serving size and diary group.

That is the whole numbered list on Cronometer's Mobile Add a Food page (Cronometer, updated 24 October 2026).

MyFitnessPal publishes six steps for iOS (MyFitnessPal, updated 23 October 2026). Lose It publishes nine (Lose It!, updated 25 August 2026).

So on the published numbers, Cronometer is already the short one. I went in expecting the opposite and had to redo the chart.

So why does Cronometer feel slow?

Because step three hides a screen full of decisions, and the page documents every one of them.

The food search carries seven category tabs: All, Favorites, Common, Supplements, Brands, Custom and Restaurants. Above them sits a Sort By menu and a database filter that can be pointed at one source such as NCCDB or a combination.

Some brand foods are then tagged with a Better Alternative, a curated swap with fuller data, and a Multi-Add toggle turns the list into tick boxes with a Review Items step (Cronometer).

Every one of those is there for a reason. Cronometer even keeps a Crono-Hacks page for people who want more of this, with recipes built out of daily supplements and custom biometrics for nutrients it does not track (Cronometer, updated 4 October 2026).

That is a nutrition instrument. If you want one, nothing below replaces it.

Which app asks you for the least?

MyNetDiary, once you use its Describe box: five published steps, on a tier that is free and ad-free.

App Steps in its own instructions Free tier Whole spoken meal Price for that route
Cronometer 4, search Yes, ads, up to 95 nutrients Voice Logging, Gold only $59.99 a year
MyNetDiary 5, Describe Yes, no ads, 108 nutrients Describe, 3 free tries then Premium $59.99 Premium
MyFitnessPal 6, search Yes, ads Voice Log, Premium only $79.99 a year
MacroFactor 6, Describe, written as prose No, 7 day trial Describe, any paid plan $71.99 a year
Lose It! 9, search Yes, Basic No, Say It finds one food $79.99 a year
MealSaid 1, say the meal Free, no purchases Yes Free

Four notes on that table. A step in a help page is not a tap on a phone, and favourites, recents and saved meals shorten every one of these counts.

Free means with ads in two cases. Cronometer puts "No Advertisements" on its Gold list (Cronometer, updated 24 October 2026), and MyFitnessPal says plainly that ads pay for its free core (MyFitnessPal, updated 15 September 2026).

Apple also never says what period MyNetDiary's $59.99 Premium purchase buys, so that row is the one price here I cannot date to a billing cycle.

MacroFactor calls its logger the "fastest food logger on the market" and writes its instructions as prose rather than a numbered list, so its six is my count of the actions in order (MacroFactor).

Can you just talk to Cronometer instead?

Yes, and both voice routes sit behind Gold at $59.99 a year.

The help page is blunt about it: "Gold users can take advantage of our AI Voice-Logging feature". You open the orange plus menu, describe the food, tap Match Foods, then tap Add To Diary (Cronometer, updated 24 October 2026).

The Siri route is the one to read before you buy. Cronometer's own getting started list runs to eleven sub-steps across three stages: install Shortcuts, enable Siri on the Cronometer shortcut, then turn on voice activation in iOS Settings (Cronometer, updated 24 October 2026).

11 setup stepsin Cronometer's own instructions before Siri logs anything, and it needs GoldCronometer

MyNetDiary's Describe costs nothing for the first three tries, then needs Premium, and it is five steps including the review (MyNetDiary, updated 21 October 2026). Our post on what each voice feature actually means has the rest.

What do you lose by leaving Cronometer?

The data quality, and most of your history.

Cronometer's free Basic account already covers up to 95 nutrients, over a million food entries and unlimited barcode scanning (Cronometer). MyNetDiary's free tier matches it on nutrient count, at 108.

What it does not match is the bookkeeping. Cronometer shows a Data Confidence figure on a nutrient target, because a branded food often carries only the fifteen or so values a US label requires (Cronometer, updated 16 October 2026).

Then there is the history. MyNetDiary's own migration page tells you to move Cronometer data through Apple Health, and lists weight, exercise and other health data (MyNetDiary, updated 3 August 2025). Your food diary is not on that list.

If depth is why you are on Cronometer, read our MacroFactor and Cronometer comparison before switching to anything.

Which one would I use?

MyNetDiary, if I wanted a database and a free account. Mine, if I wanted the meal logged and forgotten.

MealSaid is the narrow option here. You say the whole meal and it writes calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber to Apple Health, and at times you pick your phone rings and a voice asks what you ate.

What it does not do is most of this post. No barcode scanner, no food database to search, no photo logging, no micronutrients beyond those five fields, iPhone only on iOS 26, English only.

Anyone who tracks vitamins, minerals or a medical diet should stay on Cronometer. The case for a simpler app is for people whose diary is empty by Thursday, which is the failure mode the research keeps finding.

How I checked this

Checked 25 October 2026. I read eleven pages for the step counts: Cronometer's Add a Food, Voice Logging, Siri Voice Logging and Crono-Hacks articles, MyFitnessPal's logging article, Lose It's logging and pricing articles, MyNetDiary's Describe and free tier pages, and MacroFactor's two logging articles.

Prices came off each US App Store listing on the same day, where Cronometer shows Gold Annual at $59.99 and Gold Monthly at $10.99. Apple lists at most ten purchases per app, so treat those as a floor rather than a full price list.

The step counts are counts of published instructions, not timed runs on a phone. My own timed test across six apps is still unpublished, so MealSaid's one step in the table is a description of the flow and not a measurement. The Cronometer, MyFitnessPal and Lose It help centres return 403 to scripts, so those articles were read through each help centre's public API and the updated dates are the ones the API reports.
