item.title: Best free calorie tracker for iPhone: widgets, Siri, Watch
item.description: MyNetDiary's free tier documents 4 home screen widgets, 12 lock screen widgets and a Watch app that logs food. Five iPhone trackers, checked 25 Oct 2026.
item.content:encoded:
If you want the most iPhone for nothing, install MyNetDiary. Its own iPhone page claims a native Apple Watch app that logs food, 4 home screen widgets and 12 lock screen widgets, all on a free tier with no ads and no account needed.

Cronometer is the runner up with 5 home screen widgets and a Watch app that adds food, but its Siri route is locked behind Gold at $59.99 a year.

I checked what each company documents on 25 October 2026, not what the App Store screenshots suggest. I build one of these apps, so the second to last section is the one to discount.

Which free tracker does the most on an iPhone?

MyNetDiary, by a wide margin on documented iPhone features.

Its free tier page lists the barcode scanner, voice input, 108 nutrients, Apple Health sync, the Apple Watch app and Siri, describing the core version as "free and ad-free" (MyNetDiary, updated 15 October 2026).

The Watch app is the part other apps do not match. MyNetDiary says it logs foods, meals, water and quick calories from the wrist and can show any tracked nutrient (MyNetDiary).

That iPhone page is MyNetDiary selling MyNetDiary, so read its counts as the company's claim. Everything on the other four rows below comes from a help article instead.

App Widgets named for iPhone Siri that logs food Apple Watch app Widget source
MyNetDiary 4 home screen, 12 lock screen Saved My Meals, free Logs foods, meals, water MyNetDiary
Cronometer 5 home screen Gold only, $59.99 a year Add Food from recent items Cronometer
MyFitnessPal 3 named, water one is interactive None documented Water and quick add calories MyFitnessPal
Lose It! 3, including Log Foods None documented Calorie bonus only, free Lose It!
MealSaid 1 widget, 1 Lock Screen control Any meal, free Nothing I have published How it works

Each Siri and Watch claim in that table is linked in the section that covers it.

MacroFactor is missing on purpose. Its App Store listing says it "does not offer a free subscription tier" and describes a seven day trial, so nothing it does on an iPhone is free (App Store).

How many widgets does each app actually have?

Sixteen for MyNetDiary, five for Cronometer, three each for Lose It and MyFitnessPal.

Cronometer names Energy Consumed, Energy Remaining, Fasting, Water Tracking and Streaks. The water widget adds and removes glasses from the home screen, and the Energy Remaining widget carries an add food button (Cronometer, updated 22 October 2026).

Lose It names three iOS widgets: Goal Ring Calorie Countdown, Macros Breakdown and Log Foods (Lose It!, updated 6 July 2026).

MyFitnessPal's widget page names Today's Calories and Today's Macros, then adds an Interactive Water Widget for iOS 18 or later, which is the only one of its widgets that writes anything (MyFitnessPal, updated 27 August 2026).

Two of those counts are floors. MyFitnessPal's page says there are "a few options to choose from such as" the two it names, and I counted what was named.

Can you log a meal with Siri for free?

Only a meal you already saved. Of the five apps here, open ended Siri logging is paid everywhere except MealSaid.

MyNetDiary's Siri page describes built in shortcuts for calorie checks, the daily deficit, water logging and My Meals logging, added from Add to Siri buttons on the matching screens (MyNetDiary). Say the phrase and a saved meal goes in; a sandwich you invented at lunch does not.

Cronometer does take any food by voice, and it is a Gold feature at $59.99 a year. The setup list runs to eleven sub-steps across three stages before the first log (Cronometer, updated 24 October 2026).

I could find no Siri phrase that logs food in MyFitnessPal or Lose It. Both put voice behind a button inside the app, which is the whole point of the post on logging without opening the app.

Does anything reach the Lock Screen?

MyNetDiary, with 12 lock screen widgets by its own count.

Cronometer, MyFitnessPal and Lose It all document home screen widgets only, and searching all three help centres for lock screen articles returned nothing about widgets or controls.

MealSaid has a Lock Screen control, which is a different iOS thing: a button in the control picker that opens the app already listening, rather than a widget that displays numbers.

Is the free Apple Watch app worth anything?

It depends what you call logging. Two of the four will take a food, two will take a number.

Cronometer's Watch app shows the Energy Summary and has an Add Food widget that lists your most recent items (Cronometer, updated 19 October 2026).

MyFitnessPal's Watch app lets you add water or quick add calories, and feeds step data back to your goal (MyFitnessPal, updated 27 August 2026). Lose It does not take food on the wrist at all: its Watch support is a free calorie bonus from resting and active calories, and no food entry is described (Lose It!, updated 9 September 2026).

51 data typesthat MyNetDiary says it writes to Apple Health, plus 14 it reads backMyNetDiary

That read figure matters more than it looks. An app that reads nutrition back can pick up meals you logged elsewhere, which is the test in our Apple Health comparison.

Which would I put on my own iPhone?

MyNetDiary first, then mine for the meals I would otherwise skip.

MealSaid is one surface done one way. You say the whole meal, it writes calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber to Apple Health, and at times you pick your phone rings and a voice asks what you ate.

Against the table above it is thin. No barcode scanner, no food database, no Apple Watch app I can point you to, no nutrients beyond those five, iPhone only on iOS 26, English only.

MyNetDiary beats it on everything a feature list can measure, free, and anyone comparing what each free tier keeps should start there. The narrower pitch is for people who have installed three of these and logged in none of them.

How I checked this

Checked 25 October 2026. The widget, Watch and Siri claims come from each company's own help article or iPhone page, read on that date through the public help centre API where the site returns 403 to scripts. MyNetDiary's widget and Watch numbers come from its marketing page rather than a help article, so they are the company's claim, not a count I made from a phone.

I did not install five apps and photograph their widget pickers. A count of named widgets is a floor, since a company can ship one and not document it, and MyFitnessPal's page openly says there are more than the two home screen widgets it names.

MealSaid's row describes my own app. Its Siri phrase, Lock Screen control and widget are described in the earlier post, and the step counts behind the other apps' logging flows are in the Cronometer alternative post. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: MacroFactor vs Cronometer: price, nutrients and Health sync
item.description: Cronometer Gold is $59.99 a year, MacroFactor $71.99, and only Cronometer has a free tier. Nutrient counts and Apple Health, checked 24 Oct 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Cronometer Gold costs $59.99 a year against MacroFactor's $71.99, and Cronometer's free tier tracks every nutrient it has while MacroFactor has none at all. MacroFactor is the only one of the two that reads nutrition back out of Apple Health, which is the thing that matters if you ever log in a second app.

I read both help centres and both US App Store listings on 24 October 2026. Every price and feature below comes off those pages.

I build a calorie tracker myself, so treat the last section as the biased one and the rest as what the documents say.

Which one costs less in 2026?

Cronometer Gold at $59.99 a year, against $71.99 for MacroFactor.

Cronometer's US App Store listing shows two Gold purchases, Gold Monthly at $10.99 and Gold Annual at $59.99 (App Store).

MacroFactor's help centre lists $11.99 a month, $47.99 for half a year and $71.99 a year for a single app, and the same three prices appear on its App Store page (MacroFactor).

There is a fourth MacroFactor price. A bundle covering the separate MacroFactor Workouts app is $89.99 a year, and anyone who subscribed before 1 January 2026 keeps Workouts free until 12 January 2027 (MacroFactor).

Is either one actually free?

Only Cronometer, and its free account is not a stub.

A Basic account covers all 95 nutrients, the whole database of over a million entries, unlimited barcode scanning, custom meals and recipes, and device syncing (Cronometer). The limits are the advertising and a seven day window on your nutrition history, with two charts in place of the full library.

Gold buys the ad-free view, long term charts and reports, the Oracle food suggestions, fasting, custom biometrics and the recipe importer (Cronometer support, updated 17 October 2026).

MacroFactor does not do free. Its App Store listing is unusually blunt about it: the app "has a free trial, but does not offer a free subscription tier", and the same listing describes a seven day trial (App Store).

7 daysof MacroFactor before the paywall, against no time limit on Cronometer BasicApp Store

MacroFactor and Cronometer side by side

MacroFactor costs more and hands you every logging method on day one. Cronometer goes deeper on nutrients and lets you stay free forever.

What people ask MacroFactor Cronometer Source, read 24 Oct 2026
Cheapest year, US $71.99 $59.99 (Gold) MF, Cron
Monthly $11.99 $10.99 MF, Cron
Free tier None, 7 day trial Basic, no expiry, with ads MF, Cron
Nutrients documented 56 reference pages "up to 95 nutrients and compounds" MF, Cron
Barcode scanner Yes, paid only Yes, free and unlimited MF, Cron
Spoken or typed meal Describe, any plan Voice Logging, Gold only MF, Cron
Photo logging AI photo, any plan Photo Logging, Gold only MF, Cron
Siri, app stays closed Not documented Yes, Gold only Cron
Reads nutrition from Health Yes, with a priority rule Not in its docs MF, Cron
App Store rating 4.8 from 23K ratings 4.8 from 100K ratings MF, Cron

How many nutrients does each one track?

Cronometer says up to 95. MacroFactor's help centre documents 56, and I counted them one page at a time.

MacroFactor publishes a Nutrients collection with one reference article per nutrient it tracks. On 24 October 2026 that collection held 56 articles: 9 on calories and the macro breakdown, 11 amino acids, 9 kinds of fat, 12 vitamins, 10 minerals, and 5 others covering cholesterol, caffeine, alcohol, water and choline (MacroFactor).

Cronometer's Track Food page promises "up to 95 nutrients and compounds" (Cronometer), and its free tier page repeats the 95. Its own home page says 84 in the paragraph about Cronometer Pro, so their marketing does not agree with itself. Either way there is no list I could count, so 95 is their figure and 56 is mine.

Both warn you that the number is a ceiling, not what you will actually see. MacroFactor says most branded products do not report deep micronutrient data, so anything beyond calories, macros and "some major micronutrients" will be undercounted unless you log common foods (MacroFactor).

Cronometer hides some nutrients by default for the same reason, and warns that tracked values "may be significantly lower than they actually are" (Cronometer support, updated 14 August 2026).

So the real question is how many foods in each database carry a full nutrient profile. MacroFactor says 26,500 of roughly 1,360,000 searchable items are micronutrient complete, which is 1.9% (MacroFactor). Cronometer's lab analysed core is the NCC database at over 17,000 entries with data on 70 nutrients, plus USDA SR28 at over 8,000 (Cronometer support, updated 21 October 2026). Its whole database runs past a million entries and it does not say how much of that is lab analysed (Cronometer).

Cronometer does this part better. It also sells a Pro tier aimed at dietitians and research teams, which is not a market MacroFactor is chasing (Cronometer support).

Which one gets your food into Apple Health?

Both write. Only MacroFactor reads nutrition back in.

MacroFactor's integrations page spells out a priority order: manual entry, then its own food log, then Apple Health. A MacroFactor food entry for a day blocks the Health import for that day (MacroFactor).

Cronometer's Apple Health article covers activity, exercise, biometrics and sleep coming in, and tells you to pick read and write permissions, but nothing in it describes importing food logged elsewhere (Cronometer support, updated 22 October 2026).

One thing changed while I was writing. When I read that article on 20 October 2026 for our Apple Health comparison, it named the nutrient fields Cronometer writes. The 22 October version does not, and no other article in their help centre lists them now. Treat the write list as undocumented until they put it back.

Which one should you pick?

Cronometer if you care about micronutrients or want to pay nothing. MacroFactor if you want the coaching algorithm and do not mind the $71.99.

MacroFactor's pitch is its expenditure algorithm, which reads your weight trend against your logged intake and updates your targets. It needs food logged "at least four times per week, but ideally every day" to keep running (MacroFactor).

Cronometer's pitch is depth, and it charges for the fast logging paths; our voice input comparison has the detail on that.

Mine is the third option and the narrow one. You say what you ate and MealSaid writes calories and macros into Apple Health. If you forget, it calls your phone and asks.

It also has no barcode scanner, no food database to search, no Android app, no web app, no vitamins or minerals at all, and it needs iOS 26. If you want 95 nutrients, Cronometer Basic gives you them for nothing. You can read how MealSaid works before deciding.

How I checked this

Checked 24 October 2026. Prices came from the In App Purchases panel on each US App Store listing and from MacroFactor's own subscription article; Apple shows at most ten purchases per listing, so those are floors.

The 56 nutrient count is my own count of the articles in MacroFactor's public Nutrients collection on that date, so it will drift as they add pages. The 95 is Cronometer's claim on two of its own feature pages and I could not verify it item by item. Their home page says 84 for Cronometer Pro, and I did not find any page that reconciles the two.

Cronometer's help centre returns 403 to scripted fetches, so those articles were read through the public help centre API and their "updated" dates are the ones the API reports. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: 6 Cal AI alternatives that do not need a photo
item.description: Six calorie apps that log a meal with no camera, with prices read on 24 October 2026. MyNetDiary gives voice logging away free. Cal AI publishes no price.
item.content:encoded:
If you want Cal AI without pointing a camera at your dinner, the shortest answers are MyNetDiary, which gives voice logging away on its free tier, and MealSaid, which is my own app and takes a spoken sentence. Both cost nothing.

Cal AI itself is not camera-only. Its site says "Snap a photo, scan a barcode, or describe your meal", so the description route exists (Cal AI). Two of those three routes still need the camera, and all of them need a subscription.

I read every price and feature below on each company's own site or US App Store listing on 24 October 2026.

Does Cal AI work without the camera?

Yes, through the describe route, but the app is built around the photo and says so.

The App Store listing gives three steps to use Cal AI, and step two is "Snap a photo of your meal" (App Store).

The feature Cal AI sells hardest is the one that cannot work without a lens: "your phone's depth sensor calculates food volume" (Cal AI).

The same listing carries a line in capitals saying food scanning analysis requires a subscription, so the camera-free route is not a free route either.

What does Cal AI cost?

Nobody can tell you, including Cal AI. Apple lists one purchase named Unlimited at five different prices between $2.99 and $29.99.

Cal AI's website has no pricing page. What it has is a FAQ about cancelling, a FAQ about refunds, a FAQ about restoring a purchase and a button offering a three day free trial (Cal AI).

The In App Purchases panel on its US listing shows Unlimited at $2.99, $5.99, $9.99, $19.99 and $29.99, plus a $0.99 Streak Restore (App Store). Apple never says what period any of them buys.

The top price is ten times the bottom one for a product with one name. You find out which one you were shown after the trial starts.

Which apps log a meal without a camera?

All six alternatives do, and so does Cal AI. Four of them let you type into a search box for free, and only MealSaid turns a whole spoken sentence into a meal at no cost.

App Camera free route What it costs Source, read 24 Oct 2026
MyNetDiary Search, favorites, voice logging Free. AI Voice Logging is Premium Plus, $99.99 a year MyNetDiary
MealSaid Say the whole meal, or answer the call Free, no in-app purchases How it works
Cronometer Search free; Voice Logging and a Siri phrase $59.99 a year for Gold Cronometer
MacroFactor Describe, typed or dictated $71.99 a year, no free tier MacroFactor
MyFitnessPal Search free; Voice Log for a spoken meal $79.99 a year for Premium MyFitnessPal
Lose It! Search free; Say It finds one food by voice $79.99 a year for Premium Lose It!
Cal AI Describe the meal instead of shooting it Subscription, price not published Cal AI

Two rows need a footnote. MyFitnessPal's Voice Logging is Premium only, on iOS and Android, English only, app version 24.35.0 or higher (MyFitnessPal, updated 21 September 2026). And Lose It's Say It searches for one food at a time rather than taking a sentence (Lose It!).

Which free tier actually does the most?

MyNetDiary, and it is not close.

Its own feature table marks the staff verified database, unlimited search, the barcode scanner, voice logging, exercise and water tracking, up to 108 nutrient fields and the charts as free, with no ads and no account required to start (MyNetDiary).

108 nutrientstracked on MyNetDiary's free tier, with no ads and no account neededMyNetDiary

The catch is what "voice logging" means there. Free voice logging finds foods; the version that turns a spoken meal description into structured diary entries sits under Premium Plus, at $14.99 a month or $99.99 a year (MyNetDiary).

Cronometer's free tier is the other strong one: all 95 nutrients, the whole database and unlimited barcode scanning, with ads (Cronometer). Its voice route costs $59.99 a year.

If free is the whole requirement, start with MyNetDiary and read what is actually free in each app before you install anything.

Is describing a meal more accurate than photographing it?

Nobody knows, and anyone who tells you otherwise is guessing.

Photos have been measured once properly. Researchers at the NIH weighed 102 meals to 0.1 g, photographed them and ran them through four apps; Cal AI came in 345 calories low per meal, the worst of the four, and Appediet came in 252 low (Healio). Our full write up of that study has the confidence intervals.

There is no equivalent test for spoken or typed descriptions. Not for MyFitnessPal, not for Cronometer, not for mine.

What I can say is where the error comes from in both cases: portion size. A photograph does not show the oil absorbed into the food, and neither does the sentence "chicken and rice".

Which one would I use?

MyNetDiary if I wanted a food database and a barcode scanner for nothing. MealSaid if I just wanted the meal logged and gone.

Cronometer Gold sits between them: $59.99 a year buys the spoken meal plus the deepest nutrient data of the six, which is covered in our MacroFactor and Cronometer comparison.

Mine is the narrow one. You say what you ate and MealSaid writes calories, protein, carbs, fat and fiber into Apple Health. At times you pick, your phone rings and a voice asks what you ate.

It has no camera features at all, which is the point of this post, but that also means no barcode scanner, no nutrition label scanner, no food database to search and no photo logging. It is iPhone only and needs iOS 26. English only, too. On raw features MyNetDiary beats it, free, and I would say so to anyone who asked.

How I checked this

Checked 24 October 2026. Prices came from the In App Purchases panel on each US App Store listing and from each company's own pricing or feature page where one exists. Apple lists at most ten purchases per app, so those ranges are floors.

Cal AI is the one app here with no published price. I did not start its trial to find out which of the five Unlimited prices I would be shown, so that gap stays open.

The MyFitnessPal, Lose It and Cronometer help centres return 403 to scripted fetches, so those articles were read through each help centre's public API, and the "updated" dates quoted are the ones the API reports. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Lose It vs MyFitnessPal in 2026: same price, same paywall
item.description: Both charge $79.99 a year. MyFitnessPal paywalled the barcode scanner in 2022, and Lose It says it is moving its scanner to Premium now.
item.content:encoded:
Lose It! and MyFitnessPal both charge $79.99 a year, and in 2026 both put every fast way of logging behind that paywall. The thing that actually separates them is Apple Health: Lose It can read food back out of it, MyFitnessPal cannot.

I checked this because the comparison posts I found were quoting barcode scanning as a free Lose It feature, and Lose It's own help centre says otherwise. Every row below comes from one of the two companies' own pages or their US App Store listing, read on 23 October 2026.

What does each one cost in October 2026?

The same: $79.99 a year. The difference is how many other prices each one shows you.

Lose It's membership article gives one number for Premium, "$79.99 USD / Year (Auto-renews annually)", plus a Lifetime unlock at $299.99, or $229.99 for an active Premium member (Lose It! help centre). New users get a 7 day Premium trial.

MyFitnessPal's US App Store listing shows ten purchases at four distinct prices: $9.99, $19.99, $49.99 and $79.99, with $79.99 attached to three separate yearly SKUs (App Store).

Lose It's listing shows ten purchases at seven distinct prices for subscriptions, from $9.99 to $79.99, plus two more named Premium Lifetime at $49.99 and $59.99 (App Store). Those two do not match the $299.99 in the help centre, and I cannot reconcile them.

Lose It and MyFitnessPal, line by line

Eleven things people actually ask about, each cell read off a MyFitnessPal or Lose It page on 23 October 2026.

What you get Lose It! MyFitnessPal
Annual paid tier $79.99 $79.99
One-time purchase Lifetime, $299.99 None offered
Free trial of the paid tier 7 days No length stated in the help centre
Barcode scanner Moving to Premium, mid transition Premium since 1 October 2022
Photo logging Snap It, Premium, English only Meal Scan, Premium, English only
Voice logging Say It, Premium, English only Voice Log, Premium, English only
Logging a future day Premium Premium
Food out to Apple Health Yes Yes, minus caffeine and vitamin A
Food back in from Apple Health Yes, dietary energy No
Logging reminders None in the help centre Push, one per meal
Free tier pays with Promos only Premium can switch off Banner and sponsored ads

Can you still scan a barcode without paying?

Not in MyFitnessPal since 1 October 2022, and Lose It is in the middle of making the same change.

MyFitnessPal states it flatly: as of 1 October 2022, Barcode Scan requires a Premium subscription (MyFitnessPal help centre). That one is old news.

Lose It is the new part. Its article on unlocking the scanner says Scan It and the nutrition label scanner are becoming Premium features, and that "some free members will still have access as we transition, while others will not" (Lose It! help centre, read 23 October 2026).

So your Lose It free account may still scan today and stop next month, and the roundups that list barcode scanning as a free Lose It feature are describing a state that is being retired. I had it that way in the MyFitnessPal alternatives table too, and that row needs correcting.

Snap It is Premium-only and English-only, per Lose It's own article. Meal Scan is Premium-only and English-only, per MyFitnessPal's. Neither company charges less for the photo feature than for the rest of Premium.

How much of MyFitnessPal is actually free?

Eight features out of the 33 in its own comparison table, by my count.

MyFitnessPal publishes a Free, Premium and Premium+ grid. I counted the rows on 23 October 2026: 33 features listed, 8 ticked for Free, 21 starting at Premium, 4 exclusive to Premium+ (MyFitnessPal help centre).

The eight free ones are the boring essentials: food and exercise logging, weights and measurements, your own recipes, macronutrient views, goals by percentage, diary sharing, partner app links and a printable report.

Lose It publishes no equivalent grid, which is why this count exists for one app and not both. Its membership article describes Premium in a sentence rather than a table.

Both free tiers are paid for by promotion. MyFitnessPal is unusually direct about it: the core is free and "it stays that way because ads help pay for it" (MyFitnessPal help centre). Lose It runs in-app pop-ups instead, and the toggle to switch them off is a Premium control (Lose It! help centre).

Which one fits Apple Health better?

Lose It, and it is not close, because it reads food back.

MyFitnessPal's Apple Health article gives a four-row sync table. Food goes one way only, out to Apple Health, minus caffeine and vitamin A and minus timestamps. Exercise, sleep and weight come in (MyFitnessPal help centre).

Lose It moves weight, food and exercise in both directions. Food written to Apple Health by another app shows up in your Lose It log with a heart icon, once you grant Dietary Energy read permission (Lose It! help centre).

That is the one row here with a real consequence. If you ever log from a second app, a watch or a Shortcut, Lose It will show you the total and MyFitnessPal will not. The full read and write matrix across six apps is in our Apple Health comparison.

Does either one remind you to log?

MyFitnessPal does, per meal, only when you have not logged. I could find no reminder feature in Lose It's help centre.

MyFitnessPal's reminders screen lets you add a notification per meal, and the setting is literally worded "Remind me if I haven't logged" (MyFitnessPal help centre). It is free, not Premium.

Searching Lose It's help centre for reminders on 23 October 2026 returned subscription renewal notices and fasting guides, nothing about logging prompts. Absence from a help centre is weaker evidence than a documented feature, so treat that cell as unconfirmed rather than proven false.

So which should you pick?

Lose It if your food total in Apple Health has to be real. MyFitnessPal if you want a logging reminder that costs nothing.

At an identical $79.99 a year, the paid tiers are close enough that the free tiers decide it, and both free tiers are now a search box with promotions attached. That is the honest state of play, and it is the reason this blog exists.

My own app, MealSaid, is the footnote here: free with no in-app purchases, you say what you ate and it writes calories and macros to Apple Health. It has no barcode scanner, no photo logging, no food database to search and no Android build. It needs iOS 26 and it is English only. For what is genuinely free across the wider market, see the free calorie counter breakdown.

How I checked this

Checked 23 October 2026. Every feature row came from a MyFitnessPal or Lose It help centre article read through each site's public Help Center API, because both sit behind a bot wall that returns 403 to scripted page fetches. Article update dates ranged from 1 April 2026 (Lose It's barcode notice) to 20 October 2026 (MyFitnessPal's cancellation article).

Prices came from two places: each company's own help article, and the In-App Purchases panel on each US App Store listing, which shows at most ten purchases. The count of 8 free features out of 33 is mine, made by counting rows in MyFitnessPal's published grid.

What I could not verify: MyFitnessPal's own pricing page, which returns a Cloudflare challenge to everything I tried, so there is no trial length in the table. I also could not reconcile Lose It's $299.99 Lifetime price with the $49.99 and $59.99 Premium Lifetime purchases on its App Store listing. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: How many calories off is a calorie tracker? 330 to 579
item.description: Three doubly labeled water studies put logged intake 330 to 579 calories a day under measured expenditure. The food database was off by 26.
item.content:encoded:
A calorie tracker's food database is off by about 26 calories a day. What you tell it is off by 330 to 579. Every published measurement I could open says the same thing: the numbers in the app are close, and the gap between what you log and what you actually eat is the whole problem.

I went looking for this because people keep asking me whether a bigger food database would make MealSaid more accurate. The honest answer is no, and the research is not subtle about it. Checked 23 October 2026. Every figure below links to the paper it came from.

How many calories a day is the gap, really?

Between 330 and 579 calories a day, in the three studies that measured real energy expenditure rather than asking people a second time.

Doubly labeled water is the reference method. You drink isotope-labeled water, researchers track how fast the labels leave your body, and that gives total energy expenditure without anyone reporting anything. In weight-stable people it is the closest thing to a true intake number.

Boushey and colleagues dosed 45 adults, had them photograph every eating occasion for 7.5 days, and had trained analysts estimate the calories. Measured expenditure averaged 2,932 calories a day. Reported intake averaged 2,353, "a resulting difference of 579 kcal/day" (Nutrients 2017).

Serra and colleagues ran 30 women through seven days of doubly labeled water in Zurich while they logged with SNAQ, a food-recognition app. The gap was 330 calories a day, or 12.8% low. A one-day 24 hour recall in the same 30 women was 543 calories low, 22.9% (Frontiers in Nutrition 2023).

Foster and colleagues checked Intake24, an online recall tool, against doubly labeled water in 98 UK adults aged 40 to 65. People under-reported by 25% on a first recall and 25% again on the average of three (Journal of Nutritional Science 2019).

Study What was compared n Mean gap 95% limits or spread
Boushey 2017 Photographed food record vs doubly labeled water 45 adults, 7.5 days 579 kcal/day under 53% underreported, by 1,000 kcal/day
Serra 2023 Food-recognition app vs doubly labeled water 30 women, 7 days 330 kcal/day under (12.8%) 1,504 under to 845 over
Serra 2023 One 24 hour recall vs doubly labeled water 30 women, 1 day 543 kcal/day under (22.9%) 1,803 under to 717 over
Foster 2019 Intake24 recall vs doubly labeled water 98 adults 25% under 73% under to 68% over
Evenepoel 2020 MyFitnessPal vs the Nubel reference database 50 adults, 4 day records 26 kcal/day over Not significant, p = .26
Urban 2011 Restaurant menu calories vs bomb calorimetry 269 items, 42 restaurants 10 kcal/portion over 50 items at least 100 kcal over
Urban 2010 Low-calorie restaurant and frozen meals vs calorimetry 29 restaurant foods, 10 frozen meals 18% and 8% over stated One item 200% of stated
NIDDK 2026 Four photo apps vs meals weighed to 0.1 g 102 meals 250 to 345 kcal/meal under Abstract, not peer reviewed

Is it the app's database, or is it you?

It is you, by roughly thirteen to one. The database gap is 26 calories a day and the reporting gap is 330.

Evenepoel and colleagues took 50 people's four-day food records and ran them through MyFitnessPal and through Nubel, the Belgian national food composition database. Energy came out at 1,984 calories a day in MyFitnessPal against 1,958 in Nubel, with a correlation of 0.96 (JMIR 2020).

That is a 26 calorie difference, my own subtraction on their Table 1. Put it next to the 330 calorie gap Serra measured and the database accounts for about 8% of the problem.

The same paper found the database is not uniformly fine. Sodium came out at 1,293 mg a day against the reference 2,638, cholesterol at 55 mg against 242, and fiber at 15 g against 19 (Table 1). If you track sodium, that matters a lot; if you track calories, it does not.

Why does a 12.8% average still ruin a week?

Because the average is not the error you get. Serra's 95% limits of agreement ran from 1,504 calories under to 845 calories over (Table 3).

A Bland-Altman limit of agreement says where 95% of individual measurements fall. For the photo app, a given woman's day could plausibly be 1,504 calories low or 845 calories high, and the midpoint of 330 describes nobody in particular.

Foster's numbers say the same thing in percentages. The point estimate was 25% under, and the limits ran from 73% under to 68% over (Foster 2019).

73% under to 68% overthe 95% limits of agreement for one online recall against doubly labeled water, n = 98Foster et al., 2019

Boushey put the same thing in people rather than intervals. Of the 45 adults, 53% were classified as underreporters, and that group was off by a mean of 1,000 calories a day (Boushey 2017).

Are the numbers on the menu any better?

On average yes, per item no. Of 269 restaurant foods burned in a calorimeter, 50 held at least 100 calories more than the menu claimed (Urban 2011).

Urban and colleagues bought food from 42 randomly selected quick-serve and sit-down restaurants in three US states and measured the energy by bomb calorimetry (JAMA 2011). The overall gap was 10 calories a portion, nowhere near significant.

Then the detail: 108 items (40%) were at least 10 calories over the stated value, 141 (52%) were at least 10 calories under, 20 were within 10 either way, and 50 (19%) were at least 100 calories over (JAMA 2011). One side dish was over by 1,000 calories.

Their earlier paper picked the lowest-calorie items on each menu. Those 29 restaurant foods measured 18% above the stated value, and 10 supermarket frozen meals measured 8% above (J Am Diet Assoc 2010).

Packaged food has a legal tolerance, and it is wide. A food is misbranded only if the composite is "greater than 20 percent in excess of the value" declared (21 CFR 101.9(g)(5)). The same rule calls reasonable deficiencies acceptable, so there is no stated floor at all.

20%how far above its stated calories a US packaged food may legally sit before it counts as misbranded21 CFR 101.9(g)(5)

Do photo apps fix any of this?

No. The one controlled test I can find had four of them 250 to 345 calories low per meal (NIDDK, 2026).

Researchers at the NIDDK prepared 102 meals in a metabolic kitchen, weighed every ingredient to 0.1 g, photographed them, and ran the photos through MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, Cal AI and Appediet. The apps came in 250 to 345 calories under per meal and about 30 g under on fat (American Society for Nutrition, July 2026).

It is a conference abstract, so treat it as preliminary. I pulled the per-app breakdown apart in the Cal AI accuracy post, where the worst performer was also the best rated.

What do you do with a 330 calorie error?

Use the tracker as a consistent ruler, not as a scale. Set your target from your own logged average and your weight trend, and stop comparing it to a formula.

If you log 1,800 and the truth is 2,100, and you lose weight on that, then 1,800 in your app is your maintenance minus a deficit. The absolute number never needed to be right. What has to be stable is how you log, which is why the spread in those limits of agreement matters more than the bias.

Four things that actually shrink the gap, each one from a study above:

  1. Log the meal as you eat it. Foster's single recall was 25% under, and a recall is what you do when you log at bedtime.
  2. Log the forgotten things first. Boushey's underreporters missed 1,000 calories a day, and the items people photographed outside their provided meals were sugar sweetened beverages, coffee, tea and alcohol.
  3. Distrust the menu before you distrust the app. The calorimeter found 50 of 269 restaurant items over by 100 calories or more.
  4. Keep one logging habit rather than one accurate day. The limits of agreement are wide, so your average over a fortnight carries more information than any single total.

MealSaid is my attempt at the first of those. You say what you ate, it writes calories and macros to Apple Health, and it calls your phone at times you pick if you have not logged.

It has no barcode scanner, no photo logging, no food database to search and no Android build. It is English only and needs iOS 26. None of the portion-estimation problem above goes away, because you are still the one guessing how much rice was on the plate.

If you want a curated database and a long micronutrient list, Cronometer does that better than anything I have built. Why people stop logging at all is a separate problem, covered in the dropout research post.

How I checked this

Checked 23 October 2026. I read each paper at PubMed Central and took the numbers from the results text or the tables, not from abstracts alone or from secondary coverage. Sample sizes: 45, 30, 98 and 50 adults for the four validation studies, and 269 food items from 42 restaurants for the calorimetry work.

The 26 calorie database gap and the 13 to 1 ratio are my arithmetic on Evenepoel's Table 1 and Serra's Table 5, not figures either paper prints. The NIDDK meal study is a NUTRITION 2026 conference abstract and has not been peer reviewed, so it sits apart from the rest.

What I could not verify: any controlled comparison of two consumer calorie apps against the same weighed meals with the database held constant, which is the test that would settle the database question properly. The eCFR site refuses scripted fetches, so the regulation link goes to the Cornell copy of 21 CFR 101.9. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Is Cal AI accurate? It missed 345 calories a meal
item.description: Cal AI says it is about 80% accurate. In an NIH test of 102 weighed meals it came in 345 calories low, the biggest miss of the four photo apps tested.
item.content:encoded:
Cal AI's own FAQ says the app is "about 80% accurate". When researchers at the NIH photographed 102 meals weighed to the nearest 0.1 gram and ran them through it, Cal AI came in 345 calories low per meal, the biggest miss of the four apps they tested (Healio).

Those two numbers only agree if the average meal contains 1,725 calories. The meals in that study were ordinary plated meals from a metabolic kitchen.

I read the NIH press release, the trade coverage carrying the per-app figures, and Cal AI's own site and App Store listing on 22 October 2026. I build a calorie tracker myself, so the last section says where mine is no better.

How accurate is Cal AI?

It underestimated meals by 345 calories on average, with a 95% confidence interval of 296 to 392, across 102 controlled meals.

Olivia Charles and Aaron Hengist of the NIH's NIDDK intramural programme worked from 102 standardised meals made in the metabolic kitchen at the NIH Clinical Center, every ingredient weighed to 0.1 g. They photographed each meal, ran the photos through four apps, and compared the output with food composition tables (American Society for Nutrition).

Every app came in low. The headline was an underestimate of roughly a third of the energy on the plate.

App Calories missed per meal 95% confidence interval App Store rating Purchases Apple lists
Cal AI 345 296 to 392 4.80 from 372k ratings $0.99 to $29.99
Lose It! 333 282 to 383 4.77 from 782k ratings $9.99 to $79.99
MyFitnessPal 327 269 to 385 4.71 from 2.4M ratings $9.99 to $79.99
Appediet 252 210 to 295 4.78 from 48k ratings $6.99 to $79.99

Caveats before anyone quotes this at me. It is a conference abstract presented at NUTRITION 2026 and has not been through journal peer review (Healio). And the apps were fed photographs with no correction, which is how most people use them but not the best case.

One more thing the chart will not tell you. The intervals for Cal AI, Lose It! and MyFitnessPal overlap heavily, so this test does not establish a ranking among those three. Only the gap to Appediet at 252 comes close to separating.

Still, 102 weighed meals is a better test than any of these companies has published about itself.

Does Cal AI's own accuracy claim hold up?

Not against this test. "About 80% accurate" and a 345 calorie miss only reconcile at meals of 1,725 calories.

The claim sits in the FAQ on Cal AI's own site, unqualified (Cal AI). There is no sample size, no method and no link to data behind it.

Do the arithmetic the other way. If 345 calories is the mean error and the claim of a 20% error holds, the mean meal has to be 1,725 calories. A plated lunch is not that.

1,725calories a meal would need to contain for a 345 calorie miss to be a 20% errorCal AI FAQ

The ratings do not help you either. Cal AI holds 4.80 stars from about 372,000 US ratings, the highest of the four apps tested, while posting the largest error (App Store).

Why do photo apps miss so much fat?

Because fat is invisible in a photograph. All four apps were about 30 g of fat short per meal.

Hengist put it plainly: "These apps tend to underestimate calories, especially from fats" (American Society for Nutrition). Oil absorbed into a stir fry, butter melted into a sauce, ghee stirred through dal, dressing already tossed into a salad: none of it is visible once the plate is made.

Fat carries more energy per gram than protein or carbohydrate, so missing 30 g of it costs more than missing 30 g of anything else. Carbohydrates, the one macro you can mostly see on a plate, were estimated more consistently across all four apps (American Society for Nutrition).

Cal AI's pitch leans on hardware, saying the phone's depth sensor calculates food volume (Cal AI). Depth solves volume. It does not tell you what was poured into the pan twenty minutes earlier.

What does Cal AI cost?

$29.99 is the highest of five prices Apple lists for its Unlimited purchase, and Cal AI publishes no price page at all.

The In-App Purchases panel on the US listing shows "Unlimited" at $2.99, $5.99, $9.99, $19.99 and $29.99, plus a $0.99 Streak Restore, which buys back a logging streak you broke (App Store). Apple never prints the billing period, so none of those numbers tells you what you are committing to.

Cal AI's site offers a 3 day trial and states no price (Cal AI). Its terms mention auto-renewal without naming a period or an amount (Cal AI terms).

There is also no free tier. The App Store description carries one line in capitals at the end, that food scanning analysis results require a subscription. I went through the same panel for nine apps in what is actually free in a free calorie counter, and Cal AI was the only one whose core function is gated outright.

Is Cal AI worth it?

Not if you are buying accuracy. If you want the lowest effort way to get a number, it works, as long as you treat the number as a floor.

Here is the practical reading of the NIH result. If the pattern held across three meals a day, you would be short about 1,035 calories a day, which is more than most people's entire intended deficit.

That is a projection from a single-meal mean, not a measured daily figure, so treat it as the direction rather than the size. Even halved, it is enough to make a diary useless for the thing diaries are for.

If you want fewer calories missed, weigh your food and log it by weight. Cronometer does this better than anything I have built: lab-analysed nutrition data, a free barcode scanner and up to 95 nutrients on the free tier (Cronometer).

MealSaid, which I built, does not take photos at all. You say what you ate and it writes calories and macros to Apple Health (how MealSaid works), which moves the guess from the camera to your own description of the portion. That is a different error, not an absent one.

I have not published accuracy numbers of my own, so nothing on this page says MealSaid beats Cal AI. That test is running: weighed meals against a kitchen scale and USDA reference values, and it will go up with the raw table whichever way it falls. The gaps I can state now are that there is no barcode scanner, no photo logging and no food database search, it needs iOS 26 on an iPhone, and it is English only.

How I checked this

Checked 22 October 2026. The study facts come from the American Society for Nutrition release on the NIDDK work presented at NUTRITION 2026, and the per-app calorie figures and confidence intervals come from Healio's report of the same abstract, which is the only source I found carrying the breakdown by app. The abstract itself does not appear to be published anywhere I can link to.

The prices, the purchase names and the ratings were read directly off the US App Store listings on 22 October 2026 for all four apps. Cal AI's accuracy claim, the depth sensor line and the 3 day trial came from calai.app, and the auto-renewal line from its terms page.

What I could not verify: the average energy of the 102 meals, which no source states, so the "about a third" figure stays as reported rather than recomputed per app. Healio prints all four intervals with the larger number first, which fits differences expressed as negatives; I have shown them ascending. The 1,725 calorie and 1,035 calorie figures are my own arithmetic on the published means, with no new data behind them. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Free calorie counter without a subscription: what you get
item.description: Nine free calorie apps list 89 in-app purchases between them, $0.99 to $119.99. What each free tier still does, from the US App Store, 22 October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Every calorie counter in the top of the App Store is free to download, and nine of the best known list 89 in-app purchases between them, priced from $0.99 to $119.99. Free is the install, not the app. What matters is what the free tier still does the day the trial ends.

On 22 October 2026 I opened the In-App Purchases panel on nine US App Store listings and wrote down every purchase Apple shows, then read each company's own page on what the free version keeps.

If you want a free calorie counter without a subscription hanging over it, the shortlist is short. Cronometer and MyNetDiary hand you a working tracker for nothing, Lose It! does not, and two of the nine have no free tier at all.

I built MealSaid, which is free and has no purchases, so take my last section with the salt it deserves. The table is from their pages.

What does free actually mean on the App Store?

It means free to install. All nine apps I checked sell a subscription inside, and the listed prices span $0.99 to $119.99.

Apple shows an In-App Purchases panel on every listing, up to ten entries long. Eight of the nine apps fill all ten slots. FatSecret shows nine.

Ten is a display cap, not a count. An app selling twice that many looks the same on the page as one selling ten.

89in-app purchases listed across nine free calorie apps, 22 October 2026US App Store

Which free tiers actually track food?

Cronometer and MyNetDiary. Both keep the barcode scanner and the whole database free, which is the part everyone else charges for.

Cronometer's free features page is specific: "Unlimited use of our Barcode Scanner is included in a Basic account", along with the million-entry database and up to 95 nutrients (Cronometer). Gold buys you no ads and long-term charts (Cronometer support).

MyNetDiary goes further on paper. Its free tier page claims the barcode scanner, voice logging, 13 charts, reports across your full history and 108 nutrients, with no ads (MyNetDiary).

Lose It! is the surprise. Its App Store listing names three free basic features: calorie tracking, a weight loss plan and community groups. It puts the barcode scanner, photo logging, voice logging and macronutrients in Premium (App Store). A calorie counter whose free tier does not break out protein is a narrower product than the download button suggests.

MacroFactor is at least blunt. Its listing says: "MacroFactor has a free trial, but does not offer a free subscription tier" (App Store). Cal AI's listing carries one line in capitals at the bottom, that scanning results require a subscription, and its site offers a 3 day trial (Cal AI). Its cheapest listed purchase, $0.99, is a Streak Restore, which buys back a logging streak you broke.

Why does one app show seven different prices?

Because the panel lists what people buy, and the bigger apps run several price points at the same time. Lose It! shows seven of them under one name.

Seven separate purchases on the Lose It! listing are named exactly "Lose It! Premium", at $9.99, $11.99, $19.99, $23.99, $29.99, $39.99 and $79.99 (App Store). Its own help centre quotes one number: "$79.99 USD / Year" (Lose It! help).

The pattern repeats. MyFitnessPal shows Yearly Premium at $79.99 and at $49.99, Lifesum shows a one-year subscription at $119.99 and at $99.99, and Yazio shows 12 Months at $23.90 and at $47.90 (App Store).

The price you are shown in the app is one of several, and the renewal is the one that matters. The Lose It! help centre also sells a Lifetime unlock at $299.99, or $229.99 if you already pay for Premium (Lose It! help). I cannot reconcile that with the two Premium Lifetime purchases on the listing at $49.99 and $59.99.

Which free calorie counters show you ads?

Four of the nine declare advertising to Apple: MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, Cronometer and Yazio. The other five do not.

The declaration sits in the age rating panel of each listing, under Contains. It is what the developer told Apple rather than a test I ran, so treat it as a minimum.

MyFitnessPal is the only one that explains the trade in writing. The core of the app is free, it says, and "it stays that way because ads help pay for it" (MyFitnessPal support). Premium removes banners, sponsored posts and ads in the forums.

Cronometer sells the same thing, listing "No Advertisements" first among Gold benefits (Cronometer support). So on the two best free tiers here, one of them is funded by ads and the other says it is not.

So which one should you install?

If you want a free tracker that will still work in a year, install Cronometer or MyNetDiary. Everything else on this page is a trial with a database attached.

Pick by what you log. Packaged food means you need the barcode scanner, which rules out the free tiers of MyFitnessPal and Lose It!. Micronutrients mean Cronometer. No ads and free means MyNetDiary, on its own account.

If you are leaving MyFitnessPal specifically, the paywall history and the full price comparison are in our MyFitnessPal alternatives post.

MealSaid, which I built, is free with no ads and no in-app purchases. That is the only claim on this page I cannot show you an App Store panel for, because the listing is not public yet.

You say what you ate and it writes calories and macros to Apple Health, and at times you pick it calls your phone and asks. It has no barcode scanner, no photo logging, no database to search and no way to import food other apps wrote to Apple Health. It needs iOS 26 on an iPhone and it is English only. How MealSaid works has the detail.

Free with nothing to buy is easy when an app does less. Cronometer gives you 95 nutrients for nothing, which is more generous than anything I have built.

How I checked this

Checked 22 October 2026. I fetched the nine US App Store listings and read the In-App Purchases panel on each one, recording the purchase name and price exactly as Apple shows them, plus the advertising flag in the age rating panel. Counts are 10 for every app except FatSecret at 9, and ten is Apple's cap.

Free tier contents come from each company's own page: Cronometer's free features page and Subscription Types article, MyNetDiary's free tier page, the MyFitnessPal plan comparison, and the App Store descriptions for Lose It!, MacroFactor, FatSecret, Lifesum, Yazio and Cal AI. The Lose It! lifetime prices are from its help centre.

What I could not verify: FatSecret's own premium page returns 403 to anything scripted, so its free and paid split here comes from the App Store description instead. Lifesum and Yazio never name which features the free tier loses, so those two cells say so rather than guess.

A third-party pricing blog puts Yazio's barcode scanner behind Pro, and I am not repeating a split Yazio itself does not publish. I installed none of these apps for this post, so every ad claim is a declaration rather than an observation. Corrections to ohmbrock42@gmail.com.

item.title: Calorie tracker with voice input: what you actually get
item.description: Voice input means three different things in calorie apps. Seven iPhone trackers compared on 21 October 2026, and five charge a median of $79.99 a year.
item.content:encoded:
"Voice input" in a calorie app means one of three different things, and only the third saves you any real time: dictating into a search box, speaking one food into a search, or saying a whole meal that comes back as several diary entries. Of the six iPhone trackers I found with that third kind, five charge for it, a median of $79.99 a year.

I read each app's own help pages and US App Store listing on 21 October 2026 rather than trusting the marketing word "voice". MealSaid is my app, so treat the other six rows as careful docs reading and not a hands-on test.

What does voice input mean in a calorie app?

Three levels, and apps use the same word for all of them. Level one is the iOS Dictate key, level two is a microphone that searches for one food, level three is a spoken sentence that becomes a set of entries.

Level one costs nothing and belongs to Apple, not the app. Any app with a text field gets it, because the keyboard has a Dictate key (Apple). You still search, and you still pick the match and the serving.

Level two is a microphone button wired to the same search. Lose It calls it Say It, and its own logging guide puts it plainly: "use Say It to search for a food by voice" (Lose It).

Level three is the one people picture when they imagine talking to a tracker. You say the sentence you would say to a friend, and the app hands back several foods at once.

Which calorie apps let you speak a whole meal?

Six that I could confirm from their own documentation: MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, MyNetDiary, MacroFactor, Lifesum and MealSaid. Lose It has voice, but only the search kind.

App What speaking does App stays closed? What it costs Source
MyFitnessPal Voice Log turns a spoken sentence into database matches you edit before saving No Premium, $19.99 a month or $79.99 a year Help, App Store
Lose It! Say It searches the food database for one food by voice No Premium, $79.99 a year Tiers
